svg.title: OSPF network types as a design variable, with the three scenarios where the default is wrong
svg.desc: Five rows describe the OSPF network types: broadcast elects a DR with ten and forty second timers and suits Ethernet; point-to-point elects no DR, uses ten and forty second timers and suits serial links, point-to-point Ethernet and GRE tunnels; point-to-multipoint elects no DR, uses thirty and one hundred twenty second timers and suits the hub side of a hub-and-spoke; nonbroadcast elects a DR and needs manual neighbour configuration; point-to-multipoint nonbroadcast elects no DR and suits designs without multicast. A lower panel gives three scenarios where the default type is wrong: a multipoint GRE hub where one spoke gets elected DR and spoke-to-spoke traffic detours, which should be point-to-multipoint; two routers directly connected over Ethernet where the DR election is meaningless and costs one extra LSA, which should be point-to-point; and a server SVI where a DR is genuinely needed, so broadcast stays. A note says point-to-point is a zero cost optimisation because it removes the Type 2 LSA and the election.
svg.text: Network type is a design variable, not something the router detects for you
The type decides whether a DR is elected, which timer profile applies, and how many LSAs the segment costs
serial links, routed Ethernet between two devices, GRE tunnels
NBMA; the hub side of a hub-and-spoke (mGRE, DMVPN)
manual neighbour configuration required — legacy Frame Relay
hub-and-spoke where multicast is not available
mGRE hub, spokes in one subnet
Broadcast elects a spoke as DR, so spoke-to-spoke traffic detours through it
DR/BDR election is meaningless and buys one extra Type 2 LSA every change
Not wrong at all — there are many devices on the segment and a DR is the point
Zero-cost optimisation: point-to-point removes the Type 2 LSA and the election. Across a few hundred routed interconnections that is a few hundred LSAs and the SPF work they cause.
